content: The memory model will distinguish between three key node attributes: 'Importance', a static score assigned at creation; 'Relevance', calculated dynamically during retrieval; and 'Activation', a score that decays over time. To preserve historical significance, decay will only affect the 'Activation' score, not the static 'Importance'. Highly important items may have a decay 'floor' to prevent them from being completely forgotten.
rationale: This defines the core mechanics of memory node state, including durability and the forgetting mechanism, by separating static importance from dynamic activation.

content: Two competing architectural models for the memory hierarchy are being considered. A time-based model would structure the hierarchy based on meeting chronology, creating new L1 nodes for each mention of a topic. In contrast, a topic-based model would organize nodes by semantic themes, updating a single existing L1 node with new information and a timestamp to create an evolutionary history.
rationale: This outlines a fundamental architectural debate between chronological and semantic organization, which has major implications for how the system handles revisited topics and information evolution.

content: The system will incorporate a human-in-the-loop feature allowing users to inspect and manually adjust the 'importance' score of memory nodes.
